questions: Does mass 0.4 kg reduce max_error on the s-bend and slalom below the 0.06 m floor, compared with 0.6 kg in iteration 7?
Does steering_oscillation rise above about 0.17 on the slalom with the lighter body? If so, is that from higher yaw gain or from less grip?
Does line_loss_events fall to 0 on the s-bend and slalom? If not, where on the track does the loss occur?
Is progress still limited by the controller's gain or base speed rather than by geometry? If geometry is no longer binding, should wheel_radius change for ground speed?
feedback_request.requested_changes_if_any: If the slalom oscillates heavily at 0.4 kg, suggest a mass between 0.4 and 0.6 kg (for example 0.5 kg). If max_error is still pinned at 0.06-0.066 m with no change, state whether wheel_radius should be reduced to 0.025 m to cut top speed and help the controller hold the line.

intent: Change only mass, from 0.6 to 0.4 kg, on top of the iteration 7 design (0.08 m track, seven sensors at 20 mm spacing, y = 0.07 m, 12 mm footprints). The aim is to lower yaw inertia so the robot can correct faster at the 0.06 m floor. Expected: max_error below about 0.06 m on the s-bend and slalom, line_loss_events falling toward 0, and progress above the iteration 7 values (s-bend about 0.18, slalom about 0.115). Steering oscillation should stay at or below about 0.17.
learning: Track width is at its 0.08 m minimum and body width is irrelevant under the 0.06 m floor, so the active geometry levers are now mass and wheel_radius. Sensor lead, span and footprint are settled. The next result will show whether yaw inertia (mass) is still a binding constraint.
rationale: Iteration 7 is the best result so far (67.95). Narrowing wheel_track from 0.10 to 0.08 m lifted the oval to 84.1 with zero line losses, and it raised the s-bend and slalom modestly. Every development run still ends off track, with max_error about 0.062-0.066 m, just past the fixed 0.06 m floor. Body width cannot relax that floor: max(0.06, 0.0125 + 0.18/4) is still 0.06 m. Sensor lead (y = 0.07 m), span (seven sensors at 20 mm spacing, +/-0.06 m) and footprint (12 mm) have all been tested, and the 16 mm footprint did not help. Wheel_track is already at its 0.08 m minimum, so yaw authority can't be increased further through track width. Mass is the remaining yaw-response lever: yaw inertia is mass*(L^2+W^2)/12, so a lighter body turns more readily for the same wheel difference. Iteration 1 changed mass together with track and showed only a small effect, but that change was confounded with a wider track. I now isolate mass by moving it from 0.6 to the 0.4 kg minimum, keeping the sensor row and the 0.08 m track from iteration 7. Expected result: lower yaw inertia gives faster correction at the floor error, so max_error and steering oscillation fall on the s-bend and slalom, and line_loss_events trend toward 0. Risk: the lighter body may carry less grip, and the slalom may oscillate more.
